lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Coastal Marine Services | Diesel Mechanic | Lake City, USA | Jul 2025 - Present
- Rebuilt diesel engines and gearboxes for a fleet of 14 commercial fishing vessels, keeping dry-dock time under 5 days per job.
- Maintained hydraulic winch systems and logged service records for the harbor authority's annual inspections.
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Prioritized the dispute roadmap with RICE, scoring Reach as the number of support tickets each feature would close.
- After interviewing 25 merchants, mapping chargeback reasons, sizing the loss by segment and drafting a business case with finance, set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran the checkout A/B test with randomization by session and reported the 5-point conversion lift as the effect on merchants' customers.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Rebuilt weekly carrier scorecards used by 6 regional managers to renegotiate contracts, cutting late deliveries from 11% to 7% in two quarters.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites; my redesign of the slotting rules was rolled out with the floor supervisors and 45 retrained pickers.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.

- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots while rewriting the standard operating procedures, running driver training and taking over vendor negotiations for the telematics contract, which saved 1,800 driver hours a year across the region.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Raised weekly active users from 400 to 1,150, a 150% increase, by adding pickup reminders chosen after 60 user interviews.
- Raised the pickup-slot fill rate by 20% across two dining halls, from 75% to 95%, by setting up a volunteer shift system.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Patient intake at 4 clinics was mapped and the intake form was shortened, with the changes adopted by front-desk staff.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing, Python
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: Projects should appear before Experience.
items.because: Readers encounter the current diesel-mechanic role before the product-related MBA work.

items.says: The Coastal Marine Services entry gives too much emphasis to diesel mechanics as the résumé’s current direction.
items.because: The current role may make that direction appear more prominent than the product-related work elsewhere.

items.says: The bullet uses past tense for a current role.
The bullet uses past tense for a current role.
items.because: “Maintained” and “logged” make current work sound completed.

items.says: The hydraulic-winch maintenance task is not specified.
items.because: A reader cannot distinguish routine servicing from a repair or inspection task.

items.says: The bullet gives no maintenance or inspection outcome.
items.because: A reader cannot judge whether the work improved reliability or supported a specific inspection result.

items.says: The RICE bullet does not name the initiative selected or what the decision changed.
items.because: It shows the process but not the product decision or its impact.

items.says: The Reach phrase sounds like a definition rather than an account of how the scoring method was applied.
The two roadmap bullets repeat priority-setting without clarifying whether the decisions were distinct.
items.because: They may look like the same accomplishment presented twice.

items.says: The long list of methods buries the roadmap decision.
items.because: The reader reaches the decision only after four research and business-case activities.

items.says: The roadmap priority is not named.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what initiative was chosen.

items.says: The loss analysis has no estimate or comparison.
items.because: Its scale and relevance to the decision remain unclear.

items.says: Session-level randomization does not establish an effect on distinct customers.
items.because: Customers with multiple sessions may encounter different variants, so the design supports a session-level estimate instead.

items.says: The checkout test and five-point lift repeat the preceding bullet.
items.because: Repeating the same result makes it less distinctive.

items.says: The conversion event and comparison are not identified.
items.because: A reader cannot tell exactly what the five-point change measures.

items.says: The first-person pronoun is out of place in the résumé bullet.
The 1,800-hour saving appears after a long list of activities.
items.because: A scanning reader must get through several tasks before reaching the strongest evidence of value.

items.says: The disposal phrase is wordy and passive.
The user increase is 187.5%, not 150%.
items.because: The increase of 750 is 187.5% of the starting figure of 400.

items.says: The strongest accomplishment is not positioned first in the project entry.
items.because: Leading with the before-and-after weekly active user counts would bring the result into view sooner.

items.says: The interview phrase does not explain how the interviews informed the reminders.
The percentage repeats information already shown by the user counts.
The fill rate rose by 20 percentage points, not 20%.
items.because: The difference between 75% and 95% is 20 percentage points; the relative increase is about 26.7%.

items.says: The stated percentage duplicates the change shown by the before-and-after rates.
“Based on the model” repeats the basis already stated.
The savings estimate gives no comparison or analytical basis.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what the estimate was compared with or how it was derived.

items.says: The intake work is written passively.
items.because: The phrasing hides who mapped and shortened the process.

items.says: The intake change has no measure of its size or effect.
items.because: A reader cannot tell how much the form changed or what improved for patients or staff.

items.says: The recommendation’s analytical basis is not stated.
items.because: Approval shows acceptance but not what analytical work supported the recommendation.

items.says: “Final” adds no useful information.
items.because: It does not explain the work or change the action or outcome.

items.says: The pilot’s intended or achieved result is not stated.
The scheduling-pilot approval or funding outcome repeats the preceding bullet.
